summary: Jacob pauses on the journey to Egypt, remembers Bethel, and seeks assurance before leaving; God promises to accompany him, make a nation there, and return him for burial. The household travels toward Goshen, and an extended list names the family by its maternal branches, gives totals, and records deaths within that counted household.
whyItMatters: Migration for survival is placed under a promise that preserves the family's connection with the ancestral land. The genealogy presents continuity and a total of seventy, but its names and counting require attention to the hosted text's own tensions.

context.author: In the book's Sinai frame an angel recounts this material to Moses. That narrative speaker is distinct from the historical author, whom this chapter does not identify.
context.audience: Moses receives the account inside the story for Israel and its descendants. The historical work addresses Jewish concerns about covenant, inherited stories, and observance; a specific first community is uncertain.
context.date: The narrative uses a chronology counted from creation within its Sinai revelation frame. The historical work is usually placed in the second century BCE; an exact composition date is not established.
context.setting: The Well of the Oath during famine, the route into Egypt, and Goshen as the designated place for the household and cattle.
context.literaryForm: Journey and reassurance narrative followed by a structured household genealogy and numerical summary.

before.text: Jacob has learned that Joseph lives and has resolved to see him before dying. Joseph has sent wagons and provisions for the journey.

here.text: Before the genealogy, the divine speech answers Jacob's fear about going to Egypt and links departure with future burial in the land.

after.text: Joseph meets Jacob in Goshen, supports the family through famine, and eventually sees his father buried in the ancestral cave.

outline.heading: Jacob pauses and seeks a vision
outline.note: Remembering Bethel, he fears departure and observes a first-fruits festival using old grain.

outline.heading: Permission and promise for Egypt
outline.note: God promises presence and return, and Judah goes ahead to examine Goshen.

outline.heading: Leah’s descendants
outline.note: The genealogy lists sons and grandchildren and gives a household subtotal.

outline.heading: Zilpah’s descendants
outline.note: Gad’s and Asher’s households are named and combined with the preceding group.

outline.heading: Rachel’s descendants
outline.note: Joseph’s Egyptian-born children and Benjamin’s sons enter the count.

outline.heading: Bilhah’s descendants and the total
outline.note: Further names and deaths accompany the stated total of seventy and a concluding comparison.

keyVerses.text: I will go down with thee, and I will bring thee up (again), and in this land shalt thou be buried, and Joseph shall put his hands upon thy eyes. Fear not; go down into Egypt.'
keyVerses.why: The promise joins God’s presence in Egypt, Joseph’s care at death, and Jacob’s burial in the land.

keyVerses.text: And this was the goodliest (land) in the land of Egypt, and near to him, for all (of them) and also for the cattle.
keyVerses.why: Goshen is chosen with both the household and its animals in view.

keyVerses.text: And all the souls of Jacob which went into Egypt were seventy souls. These are his children and his children's children, in all seventy, but five died in Egypt before Joseph, and had no children.
keyVerses.why: The chapter explicitly states the total of seventy while acknowledging deaths within the family account.

questions.question: Why hesitate after deciding to see Joseph?
questions.answer: Jacob remembers the Bethel dream and fears going down to Egypt. He waits for a vision about whether to stay or go, so the promise of protection is sought before he completes the journey.

questions.question: How can Jacob celebrate first-fruits during a famine?
questions.answer: The chapter explicitly says he uses old grain because no fresh seed remains in Canaan. The observance therefore continues amid scarcity without pretending that a normal new harvest has occurred.

questions.question: What does God promise about Jacob’s return?
questions.answer: God promises to go down with him and bring him up, then specifies burial in the land and Joseph's presence at his death. Within this speech the return includes his body being brought back, rather than a promise that he will resume ordinary life in Canaan.

questions.question: Why choose Goshen?
questions.answer: Joseph wants the family near him, and the narrator calls it the best land for both people and cattle. Judah is sent ahead to examine it before the household settles.

questions.question: What does “souls” mean in the totals?
questions.answer: It counts members of the household as persons. The list groups sons and descendants by the women associated with each family branch, rather than offering a discussion about immaterial souls.

questions.question: Should the genealogy be treated as an uncomplicated passenger list?
questions.answer: The text includes Joseph's sons already born in Egypt and even a notice of a child born after the famine, while also saying seventy went down. These features show that the account combines household reckoning with journey language, and its stated total should not conceal those details.

questions.question: What should a reader do with the surprising opening “from Haran”?
questions.answer: That is the wording of the hosted verse, even though the chapter then places the stop at the Well of the Oath and speaks of Canaan's famine. The guide preserves the reading rather than silently replacing the place name or inventing an extra journey to resolve it.

questions.question: Does the list give every named descendant an enduring line?
questions.answer: No. It expressly records deaths among Dan's sons, the death of Iv, and Er and Onan's childlessness. The genealogy therefore includes loss and interrupted lines as well as the continuity represented by its total.

glossary.def: The harvest observance celebrated here with old grain because famine has left no new supply.
The Egyptian region selected for Jacob’s household and livestock, described as close to Joseph.
Persons counted within the named household branches and the chapter’s overall total.
